extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers interested in 19th-century literary criticism, poets, essayists, and public speakers
extracted.subtask_description: Brief, example-driven guidance on composing authentic poetry, clear prose, and effective public speeches — covering suitability of thought to form, naturalness, avoidance of sentimentality, clarity, attention, and a mock 'argymunt' speech structure. Drawn from a 19th-century literary-essay / comic-poetic context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of thought to verse
rubrics_metrics.description: “Unless one's thought pack more neatly in verse than in prose, it is wiser to refrain. Commonplace gains nothing by being translated into rhyme.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only write poetry when the thought naturally fits the verse form; do not convert commonplace ideas into rhyme simply because of the form. The passage also illustrates this with the caution that writing sentimental elegies or contrived verse (e.g., an overworked 'My Mother's Grave') does not improve the underlying material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of feeling — avoid simulated feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: “Beware of simulated feeling; it is hypocrisy's first cousin; it is especially dangerous to a preacher… the deepest grief instinctively hides its face with its hands and is silent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional expression in writing (and especially in public or pulpit contexts) must be genuine. Performative or manufactured pathos signals unreality; true sorrow or passion is often quiet. Sentimentality or 'watering' of emotion does not improve the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide between saying everything or omitting the unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: “I would put all poets on oath whether they have striven to say everything they possibly could think of, or to leave out all they could not help saying.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should choose a consistent discipline: either compress and include the essential (say everything you must) or omit what is superfluous. Avoid diffuse, over-explanatory writing that piles on nonessential material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use verse as exercise to improve prose; avoid 'bewitched' prose
rubrics_metrics.description: “The writing of verses is a good rhetorical exercitation, as teaching us what to shun most carefully in prose. For prose bewitched is like window-glass with bubbles in it, distorting what it should show with pellucid veracity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practicing verse can clarify what to avoid in prose (ornamental excess, distorted diction). Prose should aim for pellucid veracity — clarity and truthful presentation — and not be 'bewitched' by distracting ornaments that distort meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness / freshness (Nature) in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: “In litterytoor the only good thing is Natur… Thet the best of perfooms is jest fresh air, _fresh air_ … that's wut I call natur in writin', and it bathes my lungs and washes 'em sweet whenever I git a whiff on 't.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value plain, fresh, natural expression over contrivance or artifice. Writing that reads like 'fresh air' feels invigorating and honest; strive for spontaneity and simplicity that convey life rather than mannered effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial voice and personality lend weight
rubrics_metrics.description: “I am often struck… with the obviousness and familiarity of a great writer's thoughts, and the freshness they gain because said by him. … It is the advantage of fame that it is always privileged to take the world by the button, and a thing is weightier for Shakespeare's uttering it by the whole amount of his personality.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A writer's individuality and authority can make familiar or obvious ideas feel fresh and important. Cultivate a distinctive voice; reputation and persona affect how content is received, so part of effective writing is the manner of utterance, not just the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention and concentrated focus as the craft's foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: “People are apt to confound mere alertness of mind with attention. … Attention is the stuff that memory is made of, and memory is accumulated genius.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplined attention (not mere distractible alertness) is essential to developing memory, skill, and creative depth. Writers should cultivate concentration as a practical virtue underlying good work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical speech structure (the 'Argymunt')
rubrics_metrics.description: A stepwise, folksy model of public speaking: Introducshin (may be skipped); begin by talking about oneself; win the audience's goodwill by local references; introduce a seasonal or apt anecdote; state the subject; expand, delay, extend; 'pump' (energize) the delivery; restate the subject to avoid mistakes; offer gentle remarks and carry the thread forward; re-state, dilute, stir up; pump again; return to origin; engage opponents or imaginary antagonists; give a strong dressing and feel satisfied; get into other opponents' 'hair' and try other approaches; finally conclude (and possibly read extras).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This comic-but-concrete blueprint lists the common moves of a populist extemporaneous speech: open with self or local touch, repeat and reframe the subject many times, use lively pacing ('pump'), intersperse anecdotes and audience cues, attack or tease opponents for effect, and conclude by circling back. The list is presented as a procedural pattern rather than a prescriptive single style—useful as a checklist for extempore oral rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize substance over outward forms or symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: “I observe that men set most store by forms and symbols in proportion as they are mere shells. It is the outside they want and not the kernel. What stores of such do not many… lay up for the spiritual winter-supply of themselves and their children! I have seen churches that seemed to me garners of these withered nuts, for it is wonderful how prosaic is the apprehension of symbols by the minds of most men.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse ornament, ritual, or rhetorical shells with substantive meaning. In both religious and literary contexts, the temptation is to prize form over content; good writing seeks the kernel rather than the empty symbol.
